findings.passage: The in-person process gives the opportunity for informal authentication of who the voter is.  Poll workers often have personal knowledge of the voter.
findings.note: In a post on the 2020 temporary vote-by-mail bill, he describes how Massachusetts polling places confirm who a voter is, through poll workers who often know the voter, with no mention of a photo ID requirement.
subjects: in-person identity check at the polls
who is the voter: poll worker knowledge

findings.passage: A person will not receive a ballot mailed to them unless they confirm their address by returning the ballot application.    This will provide stronger protection for the integrity of the process.
findings.note: He explains why the 2020 bill had voters apply for a mail ballot instead of having ballots mailed to every listed voter, citing outdated voter lists and fraud risk or the perception of it.

findings.passage: As voters arrive in person and check in, their names are checked off on a copy of the voting list.
findings.note: In a post on how Massachusetts elections are secured, he describes in-person check-in by name against the voting list, and absentee envelopes that carry the voter's name and signature. He does not mention photo ID or proof of citizenship.

findings.passage: Finally, the bill requires the Commonwealth to start working with the Electronic Registration Information Center and share data with other states to identify people who have moved, remove them from their old addresses, and help them re-register in their new addresses.
findings.note: In his post describing the Senate voting package, he describes its voter-roll data-sharing provision. The post lists mail-in voting, early voting and same-day registration; it does not mention ID.

findings.passage: I actually do not favor allowing non-citizens to vote.  Voting is the core privilege that comes from citizenship — it is available to those who have made a permanent commitment to our country through becoming citizens.
findings.note: His reply to a commenter on his post about state voting-rights bills. It is about who may vote, not about proof of citizenship. Some commenters on the same post called for voter ID; he did not answer them on that point.
